newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Hague conference to launch chemical weapons agency.
newsitem.headline: Hague conference to launch chemical weapons agency.

text.p: Representatives of more than 160 countries will meet in The Hague this week to launch a new agency charged with enforcing a global ban on chemical weapons.
The treaty banning the development, production, stockpiling and use of chemical weapons came into force on April 29, just a few days after ratification by the U.S. Senate.
So far almost 90 countries have ratified the treaty, thus securing the right to vote at the three-week conference which will be opened by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Tuesday.
One of the conference's top priorities will be to set a budget for the new agency, known as the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW).
It will also elect a 41-member executive council to supervise the OPCW's work and will appoint a director general to run the organisation from its headquarters in The Hague.
A further 70 countries have signed the treaty but not yet ratified it and while they may attend the conference, they are not allowed to vote nor be elected to the executive committee.

These countries include Russia, whose parliament has postponed approval of the treaty until later this year, despite pressure from President Boris Yeltsin, arguing Russia needs more time and Western financial aid to destroy its chemical weapons.

Russia and the United States are the two biggest holders of chemical weapons, with combined stocks of 70,000 tonnes, and diplomats involved in setting up the OPCW had originally hoped to get both countries on board before the ban entered force.
In fact both countries almost missed the boat. Senate hawks threatened to block U.S. ratification, which eventually came just five days before the ban took effect.
Ian Kenyon, a Briton who has headed the forerunner organisation to the OPCW, admitted to some disappointment but was relieved to have at least one of the big two on board.
"We really wanted to have the two declared possessors -- the two big states in world security -- in there, but half a loaf is better than no bread at all," he told Reuters.

The OPCW is currently training a force of 140 inspectors for its core task of monitoring compliance with the treaty, which contains tough verification measures and is the first multilateral agreement to outlaw an entire category of weapons.
Member states must destroy their chemical weapons within 10 years and provide detailed information about the production and export of listed chemicals used to make such weapons.
They are barred from supplying listed chemicals to non-members and must open their chemical plants to the OPCW both for routine and short-notice challenge inspections.
Any member state which suspects a treaty violation can call for a challenge inspection, which can only be blocked if at least three-quarters of the executive council votes against it.
If an inspection confirms a violation, the offending country faces expulsion from the OPCW and possible U.N. sanctions.

Countries outside the treaty -- such as Iraq, Libya, North Korea and Syria -- are not only conspicuous by their absence but could also face problems obtaining listed chemicals needed by their industries for legitimate purposes.
Many of the so-called precursors used to make chemical weapons also have mundane, non-lethal uses in products such as medicines, dyes and weed-killers.
Even staunch advocates of the chemical weapons treaty admit its verification system can never be 100 percent watertight, but they insist it is tough enough to deter and isolate cheats.
The OPCW estimates that a budget of some $50 million is needed for 1997, its first year of operation, and so far it has been operating on advance contributions from member states.
A spokesman said the OPCW faced no immediate cash problems and was optimistic that an adequate budget would be approved.
